main.summary: The stele first tells who the filial daughter Cao E was of the Eastern Han and how she threw herself into the river to find her drowned father. It then gives the elegy Du Shang read at the sacrifice, praising a devotion that moved Heaven and earth, and ends with an inscription saying a temple and tomb were built so that she could be honoured as a spirit, like the two daughters of Yao.
main.translation:
The filial daughter Cao E was the daughter of Cao Xu of Shangyu. Her ancestors shared a forebear with the Zhou royal house; their later descendants fell into obscurity and so came to settle here. Xu could keep time and sing, and he danced in loose, swaying steps to please the spirits. In the fifth month of the second year of Han'an, the people were welcoming Lord Wu. Xu went up against the waves, was swallowed by the water, and his body could not be found. E was then fourteen. She wailed and longed for her father, and mourned by the water's edge for seventeen days, until she threw herself into the river and died. Five days later she came up holding her father's body. From the Han'an years down to the xinmao year, no one set up a memorial for her. Du Shang held a sacrifice and gave this elegy:
The one we mourn is a filial daughter, radiant in bearing. Her face was fair and her manner graceful; a gentle, lovely girl, whose smile was sweet. She should have been a bride in a household on the north bank of the Qia. But the great rites had not yet been performed when she lost her loving father. What is that blue sky, that she should be left with no father to lean on? She told the spirits her grief and went to the river, wailing without end. She looked on death as going home, and so, lightly and far from all, she cut off her life and gave herself to the sand and mud. Gentle filial daughter, now sinking, now floating; at times resting by a little isle, at times in mid-stream, at times drawn to the rapids, at times following the waves. A thousand men lost their voices, and more than ten thousand grieved. Onlookers filled the roads and gathered like clouds on the streets; they wept and wiped their tears, and the whole capital was stirred. So it was that Ai Jiang wept in the marketplace, and the city wall at Qi fell down; so some cut their faces before a mirror, or slit their ears with a knife; some sat on a terrace waiting for the flood, or clung to a pillar and burned. Alas for the filial daughter! Her virtue surpasses all these. If even the people of great states keep to ritual by their own care, how much more so a humble girl in a thatched hut. She stands straight without being propped, and is shaped without being carved. Crossing Liang and passing Song, one finds nothing to compare with her. We mourn this steadfast spirit, which will not change in a thousand years. Alas, how sorrowful.
The inscription says: Her name is cut in metal and stone, and can be put to the test of Heaven and earth. Through the years and the sacrifices a temple has been raised and a tomb built. Her light shines on the earth below and her name is made plain as a lady of the spirits. In life she was lowly, in death she is honoured, to the benefit of the gate of ceremony. How sad that the flower fell so soon and drifted away so early! A blossom so lovely and graceful will for ever stand beside the spirits, as the two daughters of Yao became the ladies of the Xiang. In every age she is imitated, in some measure, to show those who come after.

keyLines.line: 孝女曹娥者，上虞曹盱之女也
keyLines.en: The filial daughter Cao E was the daughter of Cao Xu of Shangyu
keyLines.note: The opening introduces the heroine, naming her home and her father.

keyLines.line: 漢安二年五月，時迎伍君
keyLines.en: In the fifth month of the second year of Han'an, they were welcoming Lord Wu
keyLines.note: This gives the time and setting: Cao Xu was drowned during the ceremony of welcoming the river god.

keyLines.line: 娥時年十四，號慕思盱，哀吟澤畔，旬有七日，遂自投江死
keyLines.en: E was then fourteen; she wailed and longed for her father, mourned by the water's edge for seventeen days, and then threw herself into the river and died
keyLines.note: The heart of the story of her filial devotion: a fourteen-year-old who mourns for seventeen days and then drowns herself.

keyLines.en: Five days later she came up holding her father's body
keyLines.note: The most moving moment of the story: after five days she surfaced, still holding her father.

keyLines.en: She looked on death as going home
keyLines.note: Describes how Cao E, searching for her father, did not fear death.

keyLines.en: Her name is cut in metal and stone, and can be put to the test of Heaven and earth
keyLines.note: The inscription begins by saying her name will last, carved in bronze and stone, and can stand before Heaven and earth.

keyLines.en: As the two daughters of Yao became the ladies of the Xiang
keyLines.note: Compares her to the two daughters of the sage-king Yao, who became river goddesses; so Cao E too is honoured as a spirit after death.

glossary.note: Today the Shangyu district of Shaoxing in Zhejiang. The Cao E River is named after her.
He could sing and dance to please the spirits, so he was probably a ritual specialist or shaman.

glossary.en: Han'an er nian - the second year of Han'an
glossary.note: A reign title of Emperor Shun of the Eastern Han; the year is 143.
This means Wu Zixu, an ancient statesman worshipped as a water spirit in the south, where he was welcomed with sacrifices.

glossary.en: Du Shang - an Eastern Han official
glossary.note: Tradition says he set up the memorial for Cao E and held the sacrifice.
A form of writing that mourns the dead, tells their life and praises their virtue.

glossary.en: Qi beng cheng yu - 'the wall fell at Qi'
glossary.note: Refers to the story of the wife of Qi Liang, whose weeping for her husband was said to have brought down the city wall.

glossary.en: Xiang furen - Lady of the Xiang
glossary.note: Said to be Ehuang and Nuying, the two daughters of Yao, who became spirits of the Xiang River after death.

main.background: Cao E was a filial daughter of the Eastern Han (25-220); the story of her drowning herself to find her father's body spread widely, and the Cao E River was named after her. The text is attributed to Handan Chun. As a work of calligraphy, the small regular script 'Cao E Stele' is traditionally ascribed to Wang Xizhi of the Eastern Jin dynasty (317-420), but the dates and authenticity of the surviving ink copy and rubbings are disputed, and most extant versions are later reproductions. The writing is dignified and antique, the strokes clear and firm and the structure open, and it is regarded as an important model for learning the small regular script of the Wei and Jin periods.
